```{python}
#| label: setup
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from hallmarkcite import report as R

andy_theme = {
    "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.linestyle": "--",
    "grid.color": "#d9d8d4",
    "legend.framealpha": 1,
    "legend.facecolor": "white",
    "legend.shadow": True,
    "legend.fontsize": 8,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.titlelocation": "left",
    "figure.dpi": 150,
}
matplotlib.rcParams.update(andy_theme)

num = lambda v, d=2: "--" if pd.isna(v) else f"{v:.{d}f}"
pct = lambda v, d=1: "--" if pd.isna(v) else f"{v * 100:.{d}f}%"
com = lambda v: "--" if pd.isna(v) else f"{int(round(v)):,}"

df = R.load_joined()
labels = R.load_labels()
source = R.load_source()
_hall_main = labels[labels["label"] == "HALLUCINATED"]
REAL_PAPER_SHARE = float(_hall_main["hallucination_type"].isin(R.REAL_PAPER_TYPES).mean())
DUP = R.duplicate_summary(labels)

STATUS_COLORS = {
    "Verified": "#1baf7a",
    "Minor error": "#e0a100",
    "Not found": "#5c6b7a",
    "Hallucination": "#d6453d",
}


def M(split, rule, col):
    return R.metrics_for(df, split, rule)[col]


def cell(split, hallmark, status):
    table = R.crosstab_counts(df, split)
    return int(table.loc[table.Hallmark == hallmark, status].iloc[0])


def type_rate(name, status):
    table = R.type_table(df, "all")
    row = table.loc[table.Type == name].iloc[0]
    return row[status] / row["n"]


def type_n(name):
    table = R.type_table(df, "all")
    return int(table.loc[table.Type == name, "n"].iloc[0])


def type_count(name, status):
    table = R.type_table(df, "all")
    return int(table.loc[table.Type == name, status].iloc[0])


def diff_n(name):
    return int((R.valid_miss_records(df)["Difference"] == name).sum())


def score_at(status, confidence):
    return f"{float(R.suspicion(status, confidence)):.4f}"


def entry(key, col):
    value = df.loc[df["bibtex_key"].eq(key), col].iloc[0]
    if pd.isna(value):
        return ""
    if col == "vc_year":
        return str(int(float(value)))
    return str(value)


def lead_author(key):
    first = entry(key, "vc_authors").split(";")[0].strip()
    return first.split()[-1]


def quoted_title(key):
    return '"' + entry(key, "vc_title") + '"'


def suffix_label():
    return ", ".join(R.valid_miss_version_suffixes(df))


FUTURE_YEAR_MIN, FUTURE_YEAR_MAX = R.future_year_span(df)
```

# Introduction

Hallmark is a benchmark for tools that check whether a bibliographic entry is real [@kim2026hallmark; @hallmarkrepo]. The release I use is version `{python} source["version"]`, commit `{python} source["commit"][:7]`. The public files are dev, test, and stress, `{python} com(len(labels))` BibTeX entries in total. I score them as one set. VerusCite was not trained on the dev file, so holding that file out does not change the check. The hidden test file is not in the public release. I left out the cross-domain file and the ChatGPT supplement, which Hallmark scores separately from the main table.

Hallmark labels each entry valid or hallucinated, and it gives each hallucinated entry one of 14 types. The types run from a DOI that does not resolve, through a real paper cited at the wrong venue, to a fully invented reference. VerusCite is the checker I run at [veruscite.com](https://veruscite.com) [@veruscite]. It looks the citation up and assigns one of four labels. Verified means a matching source was found and the metadata agrees. A minor error means the same work was found, with a small difference in the year, the DOI, the author list, or the wording of the title or the venue. Not found means the search did not turn up a matching publication. Hallucination means the citation looks fabricated, or it mixes pieces of different real sources.

The two positive classes are different questions. Hallmark counts a real paper with the wrong venue, a preprint cited as the published version, a shortened author list, and an arXiv record with the venue and year mixed together as hallucinations. Those four types are `{python} pct(REAL_PAPER_SHARE)` of the hallucinated entries, and Hallmark's own paper shows that verifier rankings move when they are taken out of the positive class. VerusCite is built to call a real paper with a small metadata difference a minor error. I also expect some invented entries to come back as not found, because the search missed them, and that label is separate from hallucination. Recall of the hallucination label will be lower for both reasons.

# What was checked

I used Hallmark's blinded entries. The blind files drop the url field, so a checker cannot treat a link as proof, and they do not contain the labels. I wrote one BibTeX file, `data/hallmark_public.bib`, with Hallmark's key as the citation key. The labels, types, and batch assignments are in `data/labels.csv`. Nothing in the BibTeX tells the checker which entries are the positive class.

I did not send that file as one document. VerusCite marks a later entry as a duplicate when its title and authors match an earlier entry, and it copies the first verdict onto the duplicate. It does that so a bibliography that lists the same paper twice is only checked once. In this file, `{python} com(DUP["extras"])` of the `{python} com(DUP["n"])` entries share a title and author list with another entry. They fall in `{python} com(DUP["groups"])` groups, and `{python} com(DUP["mixed_groups"])` of those groups contain both a valid entry and a hallucinated one. A changed venue, a future year, or a DOI that does not belong to the paper is often the same title and authors as the real record. One upload would have skipped the copy.

I split the file into `{python} com(DUP["batches"])` uploads. Entries that share a title and author list go in different files. A `{python} com(source["probe"]["n"])`-entry file from this bibliography finished in `{python} com(source["probe"]["seconds"])` seconds, and the worker stops a document at 20 minutes. The largest collision-free set is `{python} com(source["max_collision"])` entries, so each file also has at most `{python} com(source["max_per_upload"])` entries. Each entry was checked once, through the API [@verusciteapi]. The reports are:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-links
#| output: asis
jobs = R.shares()
print("| Part | Entries | Report |")
print("| --- | ---: | --- |")
for job in jobs:
    n = int((labels.batch == job["batch"]).sum())
    url = job.get("share_url") or ""
    link = f"[report]({url})" if url else ""
    print(f"| {job['batch'] + 1} | {n:,} | {link} |")
print()
print(": VerusCite reports for the collision-free uploads. The combined BibTeX file is `data/hallmark_public.bib`.")
```

`scripts/02_submit.py` uploads those batches, polls until they finish, writes a public link for each, and joins the results to the labels. Passing `--combined` uploads the single file instead. That run marks the copies as duplicates, so I do not use it for the numbers below. VerusCite bills one credit per 100 citations in a document, rounded up. These uploads are `{python} com(len(labels))` citations and `{python} com(source["credits"])` credits.

The scored set is the full public release: `{python} com(M("all", "hallucination", "n_pos"))` hallucinated entries and `{python} com(M("all", "hallucination", "n_neg"))` valid ones. Every entry in the joined file has one of the four labels. There are `{python} com(int((df.vc_status == "duplicate").sum()))` duplicates in the saved results.

# Crosstab

@tbl-cross is VerusCite's label against Hallmark's, for every public entry.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cross
#| output: asis
table = R.crosstab_counts(df, "all")
show = table.copy()
show["n"] = show["n"].map(lambda v: f"{int(v):,}")
for col in ["Verified", "Minor error", "Not found", "Hallucination"]:
    show[col] = show[col].map(lambda v: f"{int(v):,}")
print(show.to_markdown(index=False))
print()
print(": VerusCite labels against Hallmark's valid and hallucinated labels. Counts are entries.")
```

`{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Verified"))` of the `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Verified") + cell("all", "Valid", "Minor error") + cell("all", "Valid", "Not found") + cell("all", "Valid", "Hallucination"))` valid entries are verified. The false calls on valid entries are `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Minor error"))` minor errors, `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Not found"))` not found, and `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Hallucination"))` called a hallucination. @tbl-valid-misses lists every one of them.

Of the hallucinated entries, `{python} com(cell("all", "Hallucinated", "Hallucination"))` are hallucinations, `{python} com(cell("all", "Hallucinated", "Not found"))` are not found, `{python} com(cell("all", "Hallucinated", "Minor error"))` are minor errors, and `{python} com(cell("all", "Hallucinated", "Verified"))` are verified. The verified hallucinated entries are the ones VerusCite accepted. The minor errors are mostly the real papers Hallmark still calls hallucinations. The not found row is the miss the hallucination label does not get credit for. The breakdown by Hallmark type is in the recall section.

# False positives

The false positives are the valid entries VerusCite did not verify: `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Minor error"))` minor errors, `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Not found"))` not found, and `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Hallucination"))` called a hallucination. @tbl-valid-misses lists every one. Across each of those flags, Hallmark's valid label is often the part that does not match the citation, and VerusCite's flag does.

Of the `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Minor error"))` minor errors, `{python} com(R.valid_miss_version_doi_count(df))` have an incorrect DOI, with a version string appended. Every one of those suffixes is `{python} suffix_label()`. For `{python} com(diff_n(R.DOI_DIFF))` of them, the note says the suffix does not resolve and the title, authors, and year still identify the paper, so minor error is the label that rule is written to return. Appendix A names the other minor errors. A year off by one and a given name are real differences in the benchmark entry. The other `{python} com(R.valid_miss_plain_diff_count(df, R.AUTHOR_ORDER_DIFF))` are author-order calls, and I need to look at how the checker reads that field.

The entry called a hallucination, `{python} quoted_title("ed071a6dfa34")`, lists a different DOI, `{python} entry("ed071a6dfa34", "vc_doi")`. That DOI is Sehwag, Mahloujifar, Handina, Dai, Xiang, Chiang, and Mittal, "Robust Learning Meets Generative Models: Can Proxy Distributions Improve Adversarial Robustness?" The paper named in the citation is [arXiv:2110.09468](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.09468). Hallmark marks the entry valid. The citation's DOI is the field that is wrong. I would rather VerusCite had called this a minor error.

One of the not-found entries is a fake citation planted in the file, the canary string in the stress file. Hallmark marks it valid. It is not a paper. The other `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Not found") - 1)` not-found entries are real ICLR papers the search did not return.

# Recall

@fig-types and @tbl-types are VerusCite's label by Hallmark type, in Hallmark's order, tier 1 then tier 2 then tier 3.

```{python}
#| label: fig-types
#| fig-cap: "Share of each Hallmark type assigned to each VerusCite label. Types are ordered from Hallmark's tier 1 to tier 3."
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| fig-width: 9.2
table = R.type_table(df, "all")
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
left = None
y = list(range(len(table)))[::-1]
names = table["Type"].tolist()
for status in R.STATUS_LABELS.values():
    share = (table[status] / table["n"]).to_numpy()
    ax.barh(
        y, share, left=0 if left is None else left, color=STATUS_COLORS[status],
        height=0.72, label=status,
    )
    left = share if left is None else left + share
ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(names)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(matplotlib.ticker.MultipleLocator(0.1))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(matplotlib.ticker.FormatStrFormatter("%.1f"))
ax.grid(False)
ax.xaxis.grid(True)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.set_xlabel("Share of the type")
ax.set_title("VerusCite label by Hallmark type")
ax.legend(
    loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=True, borderaxespad=0,
)
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-types
#| output: asis
table = R.type_table(df, "all")
show = table[["Type", "Tier", "n", "Verified", "Minor error", "Not found", "Hallucination"]].copy()
show["n"] = show["n"].map(lambda v: f"{int(v):,}")
for col in ["Verified", "Minor error", "Not found", "Hallucination"]:
    show[col] = show[col].map(lambda v: f"{int(v):,}")
print(show.to_markdown(index=False))
print()
print(": Hallucinated entries, by Hallmark type. Tier is Hallmark's difficulty tier.")
```

The current implementation will need to be amended to better catch future dates and nonexistent venues. See Appendix B for several examples of each. Many of the other articles that appendix does not cover are intentionally flagged as minor errors, including a fabricated DOI. Hallmark's future-date entries set the year from `{python} FUTURE_YEAR_MIN` to `{python} FUTURE_YEAR_MAX` on a real paper. Of those, `{python} pct(type_rate("future date", "Minor error"))` are minor errors, and `{python} com(type_count("future date", "Verified"))` were verified by a DOI lookup whose saved note does not mention the year. Of the nonexistent-venue entries, `{python} com(type_count("nonexistent venue", "Verified"))` were verified and `{python} com(type_count("nonexistent venue", "Minor error"))` are minor errors. If the only problem is a date in the future, a later version of the checker will still flag the article as a minor error.

A fabricated DOI, with the rest of the citation identifying the paper, is one of those intentional minor errors. Of the `{python} com(type_n("fabricated doi"))` fabricated DOIs, `{python} pct(type_rate("fabricated doi", "Minor error"))` are minor errors and `{python} pct(type_rate("fabricated doi", "Hallucination"))` are hallucinations. The hallucination label is not meant to catch that case. Wrong venue and a partial author list keep a real paper and change one field. Of the wrong-venue entries, `{python} pct(type_rate("wrong venue", "Minor error"))` are minor errors and `{python} pct(type_rate("wrong venue", "Hallucination"))` are hallucinations. Of the partial author lists, `{python} pct(type_rate("partial author list", "Minor error"))` are minor errors. Near-miss titles sit in between. `{python} pct(type_rate("near miss title", "Minor error"))` are minor errors and `{python} pct(type_rate("near miss title", "Hallucination"))` are hallucinations. Plausible fabrications are the invented entries. Of `{python} com(type_n("plausible fabrication"))` plausible fabrications, `{python} pct(type_rate("plausible fabrication", "Hallucination"))` are hallucinations and `{python} pct(type_rate("plausible fabrication", "Not found"))` are not found.

I score three rules. The strict rule counts only VerusCite's hallucination label as a detection. The second counts hallucination or not found, which is the strict rule plus the lookups that did not return a paper. The third counts anything other than verified, so a minor error is also a detection. Recall is the share of Hallmark's hallucinated entries that the rule flags. The false positive rate is the share of valid entries that it flags. @tbl-rates has both, with the counts.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rates
#| output: asis
rows = []
for rule in R.RULES:
    m = R.metrics_for(df, "all", rule)
    rows.append({
        "Rule": R.RULE_LABELS[rule],
        "Caught": f"{m['tp']:,} / {m['n_pos']:,}",
        "Recall": pct(m["recall"]),
        "False positives": f"{m['fp']:,} / {m['n_neg']:,}",
        "FPR": pct(m["fpr"]),
    })
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False))
print()
print(": Recall on Hallmark's hallucinated entries and the false positive rate on valid entries. Caught is true positives over hallucinated entries. False positives are valid entries the rule flags.")
```

The hallucination label catches `{python} com(M("all", "hallucination", "tp"))` of `{python} com(M("all", "hallucination", "n_pos"))` hallucinated entries, recall `{python} pct(M("all", "hallucination", "recall"))`, and it flags `{python} com(M("all", "hallucination", "fp"))` of `{python} com(M("all", "hallucination", "n_neg"))` valid entries, a false positive rate of `{python} pct(M("all", "hallucination", "fpr"))`. The false-positive section is where that one valid entry is discussed.

Counting not found with hallucination raises recall to `{python} pct(M("all", "hall_or_nf", "recall"))` (`{python} com(M("all", "hall_or_nf", "tp"))` of `{python} com(M("all", "hall_or_nf", "n_pos"))`) and raises the false positive rate to `{python} pct(M("all", "hall_or_nf", "fpr"))` (`{python} com(M("all", "hall_or_nf", "fp"))` of `{python} com(M("all", "hall_or_nf", "n_neg"))`). The extra true positives are the `{python} com(cell("all", "Hallucinated", "Not found"))` hallucinated entries labeled not found. The extra false positives are the `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Not found"))` valid entries with the same label.

Counting minor errors as well raises recall to `{python} pct(M("all", "not_verified", "recall"))` and the false positive rate to `{python} pct(M("all", "not_verified", "fpr"))`. That rule flags every entry VerusCite did not fully accept. Most of the recall it adds, relative to the not-found rule, is the real-paper types, which the minor-error rule is written to hold.

Hallmark's published table is on the dev file alone: a DOI lookup at detection rate 0.218 and false positive rate 0.043, Gemini 2.5 Pro at 0.476 and 0.050, and bibtex-updater, which they treat as a co-designed upper bound, at 0.820 and 0.051 when abstentions are scored as valid [@kim2026hallmark]. The rates above are the full public set. Their detection rate also credits a wrong venue, which VerusCite's hallucination label does not.

@tbl-fold recomputes the rates the two ways Hallmark uses when those four real-paper types stop counting as hallucinations. Dropping them removes the entries from the scored set. Scoring them as valid means a flag on one of them is a false positive.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-fold
#| output: asis
rows = []
for mode, mode_label in [("drop", "Dropped from the scored set"), ("as_valid", "Scored as valid")]:
    folded = R.fold_frame(df, mode)
    for rule in ("hallucination", "hall_or_nf", "not_verified"):
        m = R.metrics_for(folded, "all", rule)
        rows.append({
            "Real-paper types": mode_label,
            "Rule": R.RULE_LABELS[rule],
            "Recall": pct(m["recall"]),
            "FPR": pct(m["fpr"]),
            "Hallucinated n": f"{m['n_pos']:,}",
            "Valid n": f"{m['n_neg']:,}",
        })
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False))
print()
print(": The full public set, after the four real-paper types (wrong venue, preprint cited as published, partial author list, arXiv version mismatch) are dropped or treated as valid.")
```

Under the strict rule, dropping those types moves recall from `{python} pct(M("all", "hallucination", "recall"))` to `{python} pct(R.metrics_for(R.fold_frame(df, "drop"), "all", "hallucination")["recall"])`. The false positive rate stays `{python} pct(R.metrics_for(R.fold_frame(df, "drop"), "all", "hallucination")["fpr"])`, because the dropped entries were hallucinated, so the valid count does not change. Treating them as valid moves the false positive rate to `{python} pct(R.metrics_for(R.fold_frame(df, "as_valid"), "all", "hallucination")["fpr"])`. Flagging a wrong venue is then a false alarm, which is what the hallucination label mostly avoids by putting those entries in minor error.

# A score and the ROC curve

Each entry gets one score. Verified is 0, minor error is 1, not found is 2, and hallucination is 3. Confidence is between 0 and 1, and it is how sure VerusCite is of the label it chose. I add the confidence inside that label's slot, multiplied by 0.999, so it cannot reach the next label.

For a verified entry the piece I add is 0.999 times one minus the confidence. That is the rank plus one minus the confidence, held just short of the next label. A more confident verified call scores lower. For the other three labels the piece I add is 0.999 times the confidence, so a more confident call scores higher.

An entry flagged as verified with confidence `{python} format(0.90, ".2f")` gets a score of `{python} score_at("verified", 0.90)`. An entry flagged as verified with confidence `{python} format(0.20, ".2f")` gets a score of `{python} score_at("verified", 0.20)`. An entry flagged as a minor error with confidence `{python} format(0.80, ".2f")` gets a score of `{python} score_at("minor_error", 0.80)`. An entry flagged as a minor error with confidence `{python} format(0.40, ".2f")` gets a score of `{python} score_at("minor_error", 0.40)`. An entry flagged as not found with confidence `{python} format(0.60, ".2f")` gets a score of `{python} score_at("not_found", 0.60)`. An entry flagged as a hallucination with confidence `{python} format(0.70, ".2f")` gets a score of `{python} score_at("hallucination", 0.70)`.

Every verified score is below 1. Every minor error is at least 1 and below 2. Every not found is at least 2 and below 3. Every hallucination is at least 3 and below 4.

@fig-roc is an ordinary ROC curve on that score. Hallmark's hallucinated label is the positive class. I sort the entries from the highest score to the lowest. At each distinct score, the threshold flags every entry at or above it. Recall is the share of hallucinated entries flagged. The false positive rate is the share of valid entries flagged. Those pairs are the curve. The routine is `sklearn.metrics.roc_curve`. Points that lie on the straight line between their neighbors are left off the plot. The line is the same either way.

```{python}
#| label: fig-roc
#| fig-cap: "ROC curve for the label-and-confidence score on the full public set. The marked points are the three rules, which are whole labels."
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-width: 4.8
curve = R.roc_for(df, "all")
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(curve["fpr"], curve["tpr"], color="#2a78d6", lw=1.8)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="#52514e", lw=1, ls=":")
markers = {
    "hallucination": ("o", "#d6453d"),
    "hall_or_nf": ("s", "#5c6b7a"),
    "not_verified": ("D", "#e0a100"),
}
for rule, (marker, color) in markers.items():
    point = curve["points"][rule]
    ax.plot(
        point["fpr"], point["recall"], marker=marker, color=color, ms=7,
        markeredgecolor="white", linestyle="none", label=R.RULE_LABELS[rule],
    )
ax.set_xlim(-0.02, 1.02)
ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.02)
ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate")
ax.set_ylabel("Recall")
ax.set_title("Public entries")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
```

The area under the curve is `{python} num(R.auc_for(df, "all"), 3)`. Using only the four label numbers, with confidence ignored, the area is `{python} num(R.auc_for(df, "all", fine=False), 3)`.

The marked points are the three rules in @tbl-rates. They use the label and ignore confidence. Scores of 3 or above are the hallucination label, recall `{python} pct(M("all", "hallucination", "recall"))` and false positive rate `{python} pct(M("all", "hallucination", "fpr"))`. Scores of 2 or above add not found. Scores of 1 or above add minor errors. Between those points the curve is only the confidence order inside one label. The area is larger than the hallucination label's recall because a minor error still ranks above a verified entry, and a not found still ranks above a minor error.

# Limits

This is a check of bibliographic metadata, which is also what Hallmark measures. I did not ask whether a manuscript's claim is supported by the cited paper. The public entries are mostly papers from major machine-learning venues. A bibliography of books, reports, or legal citations would land in different places, and not found would be more common for work that is real and absent from the indexes VerusCite searches.

The duplicate rule is a property of the product, not of the benchmark. A user who uploads one file in which the same title and authors appear twice will get one check. I split the file so the numbers above are one check per entry. The links in @tbl-links are that run.

Hallmark has not settled whether a real paper with the wrong venue is a hallucination. @tbl-fold is there so the rates can be read either way. I would use the hallucination label when the question is whether the reference was invented, and I would read minor errors as a separate list of metadata to fix.

# AI use disclosure

The code, the API run, and the text were produced with Grok (xAI, Grok 4.7) under my direction. I specified the benchmark, the use of the VerusCite API, the crosstab of VerusCite's labels with Hallmark's, separate sections for the false positives and for recall, the AUC, the worked examples for how that ROC score is built, the walk-through of the valid entries in those false-positive counts, the two appendices with the full citation and the checker's note, the count of version-suffixed DOIs among those valid misses, and the Figure 1 legend and gridlines. The split into collision-free batches was required by VerusCite's duplicate rule, which would otherwise have skipped entries that share a title and author list. All numbers and figures are computed from the scripts and the saved API results in the repository.

# Appendix A. Valid entries that were not verified {.unnumbered}

The false-positive section is the reading of these rows. Hallmark marks the entries in @tbl-valid-misses valid. VerusCite did not verify them: `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Minor error"))` minor errors, `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Not found"))` not found, and `{python} com(cell("all", "Valid", "Hallucination"))` called a hallucination.

A fabricated DOI is a minor error when the rest of the citation identifies the paper. I wrote that rule so a bad identifier would be a field to fix, and the paper would still count as found. An unresolved DOI is the same call. Of the `{python} com(len(R.valid_miss_records(df)))` entries in this table, `{python} com(R.valid_miss_version_doi_count(df))` append a version number to the DOI. Every one of those suffixes is `{python} suffix_label()`. For `{python} com(diff_n(R.DOI_DIFF))` of them, the note says the suffix does not resolve and the title, authors, and year match the preprint. The other `{python} com(R.valid_miss_version_doi_count(df) - diff_n(R.DOI_DIFF))` still end in that suffix, and the note names another field. `{python} quoted_title("a0527a7c2d1b")` is a preprint title that changed between versions. `{python} quoted_title("e835ddd85ea6")` is an author list: the citation matches the v1 author list, including Weiping Wang, and the note compares it with a later list.

A year off by one is a minor error for the same reason. The paper is the one cited, and the year is the field that is wrong. That rule accounts for `{python} com(diff_n(R.YEAR_DIFF))` of these valid entries, `{python} quoted_title("f34f26c83153")`. The citation says `{python} entry("f34f26c83153", "vc_year")`. The note says the ICLR page is the 2020 conference. That is a real year error. Hallmark's future-date type is a larger shift, the year set from `{python} FUTURE_YEAR_MIN` to `{python} FUTURE_YEAR_MAX`, and `{python} pct(type_rate("future date", "Minor error"))` of those entries are minor errors when the year is checked against the record.

`{python} quoted_title("f37417a49de6")` is a real given-name difference. The citation says Drew Bagnell. The note says the Microsoft Research page lists J. Andrew Bagnell.

`{python} quoted_title("e1694f2a0b29")` lists Kui Ren. That is the name on the CVPR paper. The checker's note says the IEEE Xplore page lists six authors and leaves Kui Ren off. One IEEE HTML rendering of the same record shows Kui Rent. The benchmark spelling matches the paper. The minor-error call is the short IEEE author list.

The other `{python} com(R.valid_miss_plain_diff_count(df, R.AUTHOR_ORDER_DIFF))` minor errors are author-order calls: `{python} quoted_title("b2505314787f")`, `{python} quoted_title("bcc0d3be5e64")`, and `{python} quoted_title("ea8d6b0ea3d9")`. The citation order matches the proceedings order on the pages I checked. `{python} quoted_title("b2505314787f")` puts Xing Xie before Jian Tang, which is the ICLR order, and the note says the citation does the reverse. The note on `{python} quoted_title("bcc0d3be5e64")` says the order differs and that the NeurIPS page confirms the cited order. I need to look at how the checker is reading author order.

The three not-found rows are the canary string and the two papers the search missed. The hallucination row is the DOI that resolves to a different paper. The trace is the checker's full note.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show = R.valid_miss_table(df)
print(show.to_markdown(index=False))
print()
print(': Valid entries VerusCite did not verify. The citation is the entry that was checked. The DOI links to the identifier and, where the checker stored a page, to that article. The trace is the checker\'s full note. {#tbl-valid-misses tbl-colwidths="[10,28,22,40]"}')
```

# Appendix B. Verified and minor-error samples {.unnumbered}

For each Hallmark type, the tables below draw up to five entries VerusCite verified and up to five it called a minor error. The draw sorts on the citation key and samples with seed `{python} R.SAMPLE_SEED`. A label with fewer than five entries contributes every row. Each row is the full citation, the DOI with a link to the article when the checker stored one, and the checker's full note.

```{python}
#| output: asis

def _join_types(names):
    if len(names) == 1:
        return names[0]
    if len(names) == 2:
        return f"{names[0]} and {names[1]}"
    return ", ".join(names[:-1]) + ", and " + names[-1]


def _shown(table, status):
    rows = table["rows"]
    if rows.empty:
        return 0
    return int(rows["vc_status"].eq(status).sum())


def _sample_caption(table):
    pretty = table["label"][0].upper() + table["label"][1:]
    parts = [pretty + "."]
    nv, nm = table["n_verified"], table["n_minor"]
    sv, sm = _shown(table, "verified"), _shown(table, "minor_error")
    if nv == 0:
        parts.append("No verified entries.")
    elif sv == nv:
        parts.append(f"All {nv} verified entries.")
    else:
        parts.append(f"{sv} of {nv} verified entries.")
    if nm == 0:
        parts.append("No minor errors.")
    elif sm == nm:
        parts.append(f"All {nm} minor errors.")
    else:
        parts.append(f"{sm} of {nm} minor errors.")
    return " ".join(parts)


tables = R.type_sample_tables(df)
empty = [table["label"] for table in tables if table["n_verified"] == 0 and table["n_minor"] == 0]
if empty:
    joined = _join_types(empty)
    joined = joined[0].upper() + joined[1:]
    if len(empty) == 1:
        print(f"{joined} has no verified entries and no minor errors, so that type has no table.")
    else:
        print(f"{joined} have no verified entries and no minor errors, so those types have no table.")
    print()

for table in tables:
    if table["n_verified"] == 0 and table["n_minor"] == 0:
        continue
    show = R.sample_display(table["rows"])
    caption = _sample_caption(table)
    pretty = table["label"][0].upper() + table["label"][1:]
    print(f"**{pretty}.**")
    print()
    print(show.to_markdown(index=False))
    print()
    print(f": {caption}")
    print()
```
